excerpts.text:
The IOC is touting the 2026 Games as “the most gender-balanced Olympic Winter Games in history,” with women making up 47 percent of athletes. Twelve of the 16 disciplines include full gender parity. But one discipline lacks a women’s event altogether: Nordic combined.

While women started competing in cross-country skiing at the Olympics in 1952 and ski jumping in 2014, women’s Nordic combined didn’t host its first World Cup season until 2020-21.

“The future inclusion of Nordic combined depends on significant positive developments, particularly with regard to participation and audience,” the IOC said in a statement, pointing to the fact that at the last three Winter Games, athletes from just four countries — Norway, Germany, Japan and Austria — won all the medals in the three Olympic Nordic combined events.

assessment.rationale: The article explicitly states women have never competed in Nordic combined at the Olympics (span 10), and that one discipline lacks a women's event altogether (span 13). The IOC's gender balance claim is qualified by this exclusion.
assessment.synthesis_coverage: Directly contradicts the 'fully gender balanced' claim for Nordic combined; establishes that women's Nordic combined is absent from the Olympic program.
assessment.provenance_note: Span 10: 'Women have never competed in Nordic combined at the Olympics.' Span 13: 'But one discipline lacks a women's event altogether: Nordic combined.' Span 68: IOC conditional evaluation language.
limitations: The article focuses on Nordic combined as the exception; does not address whether other disciplines meet a specific 'fully gender balanced' threshold beyond the 12/16 count
